title: Internal Firm Analysis Resources Capabilities & Core Competencies (Part 1)

questions.stem: Context: Apple’s Vision Pro Ecosystem Apple integrates custom silicon (M2/R1 chips), proprietary optics, and its OS. Meta uses third-party Qualcomm chips. Apple’s internal ability to make these parts "talk" to each other perfectly represents:

options.B: The rarity of the hardware components which are traded in a perfectly competitive global supply chain.
options.C: A cost-leadership strategy that exploits economies of scale in the primary activity of inbound logistics.
options.D: The "Organization" aspect of VRIO, as Meta is a social media company and not a hardware manufacturer.

questions.explanation: A (Resource Interconnectedness): How components work together as a system.

questions.stem: Context: Better Expectations of Future Value A land developer buys a swamp for $1M. A month later, Disney announces a park next door. The swamp is now worth $500M. This advantage is based on:
questions.explanation: A (Foresight or luck): Buying a resource cheap before its value is known.

questions.stem: Context: Core Rigidity (Nokia) Nokia was so good at hardware engineering that it ignored the shift to software-led ecosystems. Their former competency became a:
questions.explanation: A (Core Rigidity): Yesterday's strength is today's weakness.

questions.stem: Context: Corporate Culture as a Shield Why is "Company Culture" considered the ultimate isolating mechanism?

options.A: It represents a resource flow that is easily measured through standard performance metrics.
options.C: It is perfectly mobile and can be moved to a competitor if the leadership team is hired away.
options.D: It is a tangible resource protected by corporate bylaws and non-disclosure agreements.

questions.explanation: A (Causally ambiguous): Hard to explain, therefore hard to copy.

questions.stem: Context: Data Moats (Google Search) Google has so much search data that its AI improves faster than Bing's. The concept that "the more you have, the easier it is to get more" is known as:
questions.explanation: A (Asset mass efficiency): Success breeds more success (data).

questions.stem: Context: Intel’s Foundry Transformation Intel is shifting from a "Design-First" culture to a "Foundry-Service" (Manufacturing for others) culture. This is failing because the old "Internal-only" mindset prevents them from serving external clients well. This is:

options.A: A lack of resource heterogeneity within the global semiconductor fabrication and design market.
options.C: The inability to turn a tangible resource (a factory) into an intangible capability (service culture).
options.D: A failure of the "Rare" component of VRIO, as firms like TSMC already possess similar resources.

questions.explanation: A (Core Rigidity): Success in one area (Design) blocks success in another (Service).

questions.stem: Context: Luxury Watchmaking (Patek Philippe) Artisans at Patek Philippe have worked together for 40 years. A new startup, "Luxe-Time," hires 10 of these artisans away. However, Luxe-Time watches still lack the "soul" and quality of a Patek. This is due to:
questions.explanation: A (Socially complex): 40 years of teamwork cannot be hired away.

questions.stem: Context: NVIDIA’s CUDA Moat Competitors like Groq have produced chips that are technically faster than NVIDIA’s H100s. However, enterprise clients refuse to switch because their existing software stacks are built on NVIDIA's CUDA. This advantage is:

options.A: A tangible resource stock that can be purchased by any firm with sufficient venture capital funding.
options.B: A temporary competitive advantage that will disappear once the industry reaches the "Shakeout" phase.
options.D: Resulting from the resource heterogeneity of the global semiconductor fabrication and foundry market.

questions.explanation: A (Path dependent): You can't skip 15 years of software history.

questions.stem: Context: Netflix’s Content Pivot Netflix moved from DVDs to Streaming to Original Content (Stranger Things). This ability to repeatedly reconfigure its resource base to meet new threats is the textbook definition of:
questions.explanation: A (Dynamic Capabilities): The ability to reconfigure resources.

questions.stem: Context: OpenAI & The Human Capital Flight When high-level researchers left OpenAI to form Anthropic, OpenAI's valuation remained high because they retained the code. However, Anthropic struggled to replicate the specific "safety-tuning" results of GPT-4 initially. In RBV terms, this indicates the safety-tuning advantage was likely:

options.B: A failure of the VRIO "Organization" component within the original OpenAI human resource policy.
options.C: Protected by resource immobility stemming from legal non-compete clauses in the researchers' contracts.
options.D: A tangible resource flow that was built over several fiscal quarters of heavy R&D investment.

questions.explanation: A (Socially complex): The "magic" of a team is in the relationships, not the individuals.

questions.stem: Context: Primary Activities (Value Chain) For an e-commerce giant like Amazon, "Operations" in the value chain refers to:
questions.explanation: A (Warehouse sorting): Primary activities touch the physical product/service.

questions.stem: Context: RBV Assumptions If resources were "Mobile" and "Homogeneous," the result for all firms in an industry would be:
questions.explanation: A (Competitive Parity): If everyone is the same, no one wins.

questions.stem: Context: Resource Heterogeneity What does "Resource Heterogeneity" actually mean?

options.A: All firms in an industry have the same resources but different managers.
options.B: Resources move easily from firm to firm in search of the highest bidder.
options.D: Only tangible resources differ across firms, while intangible ones are uniform.

questions.explanation: A (Resource bundles differ): The core assumption of RBV.

questions.stem: Context: Shein’s Supply Chain Agility Shein uses a real-time data "brain" to command 3,000 small factories. Zara attempts to copy this but is slowed down by its existing long-term contracts with large-scale manufacturers. Zara is facing:

options.B: Causal ambiguity concerning the link between small-batch production and high-frequency data.
options.C: A lack of primary activities in Zara's value chain regarding "Outbound Logistics" and service.

questions.explanation: A (Resource Immobility): Resources (contracts) are "sticky" and don't move.

questions.stem: Context: Southwest’s Low-Cost System United Airlines tried to copy Southwest's "Point-to-Point" model but kept its "Hub-and-Spoke" baggage handlers. The system crashed. This illustrates that:

options.B: Southwest’s advantage was based on a tangible resource that United could not legally purchase.
options.C: The external environment (PESTEL) shifted toward high-cost fuel, making the model obsolete.
options.D: United failed the "Valuable" test of VRIO because point-to-point flying is not valuable.

questions.explanation: A (Capabilities are interconnected): You can't copy half a system.

questions.stem: Context: Strategic Managerial Discretion A CEO decides to sell the firm's profitable gas-engine division to bet everything on Hydrogen. This "pivoting" is an exercise of:
questions.explanation: A (Dynamic Capabilities): Choosing to reconfigure the firm.

questions.stem: Context: Tangible vs. Intangible Which of the following is an Intangible Resource?
questions.explanation: A (Reputation): You cannot touch it; it is intangible.

questions.stem: Context: The "Bathtub Metaphor" (Brand Equity) A startup spends $500M on a Super Bowl ad (Flow) to build a brand. In the following year, they spend $0. According to the bathtub metaphor, why does the brand still generate sales in the second year?

options.B: Intangible resources are more susceptible to time compression diseconomies than tangible ones like cash.
options.C: The "leakage" in the bathtub metaphor is irrelevant if the initial inflow was at a global scale.
options.D: Resource flows are the only source of sustainable competitive advantage in digital markets.

questions.explanation: A (Stocks erode slowly): Brand doesn't disappear the moment you stop ads.

questions.stem: Context: The Biotech Patent Trap Firm A has a patent on a drug. Firm B creates a different chemical "work-around" that delivers the same health outcome without infringing. In VRIO terms, Firm A’s patent provided only:
questions.explanation: A (Temporary): If someone can "invent around" it, it's not sustainable.

questions.stem: Context: The Innovation Manual Company X writes a detailed "Innovation Playbook." A spy steals it and gives it to Company Y. Company Y still fails to innovate. This is because innovation is:

options.A: A tangible resource that lacks the "Rare" component of the VRIO framework.
options.B: A resource stock that requires 20 years of path-dependent investment.
options.C: A primary activity that cannot be documented in a support activity manual.

questions.explanation: A (Tacit knowledge): "Know-how" cannot be written down.

questions.stem: Context: The Star CEO Failure A struggling retailer hires a celebrity CEO. The CEO introduces a "digital-first" strategy, but the store-level employees refuse to implement it. From an internal analysis perspective, the CEO's failure is due to:

options.A: The firm possessing a temporary competitive advantage that the CEO inadvertently converted to parity.
options.B: Human capital being a perfectly mobile resource that cannot be a source of competitive advantage.
options.D: The CEO lacking the "Valuable" component of the VRIO framework in the context of retail.

questions.explanation: A (Core Rigidity): An old way of doing things that blocks a new strategy.

questions.stem: Context: The Startup "Marketing Blitz" A startup tries to build "Nike-level" brand loyalty in 3 months by spending $2B. They fail because you cannot "rush" 50 years of consumer trust. This concept is:
questions.explanation: A (Time compression diseconomies): Rushing 50 years into 3 months fails.

questions.stem: Context: TikTok’s "Secret" Recommendation Engine US firms have the code for TikTok's algorithm. Yet, Reels and Shorts fail to replicate the engagement. The "cause" of TikTok's success is a mystery even to its own engineers, involving complex data-loops and moderation. This is:

options.B: A failure of the Resource-Based View to account for external PESTEL factors in social media.
options.C: A lack of primary activities in the competitor's value chain, specifically regarding outbound logistics.

questions.explanation: A (Causal ambiguity): If the cause of success is a mystery, it's hard to copy.

questions.stem: Context: Value Chain (Support Activities) In a company like OpenAI, which of the following is a "Support Activity" that acts as a core competency?
questions.explanation: A (Human Resource Management): Hiring the best AI minds is a support activity but a core competency for OpenAI.

questions.stem: Context: Xerox PARC & The Mouse Xerox invented the PC and the Mouse but never made a profit from them. They had the resources (V, R, I) but lacked the business units to market them. Xerox failed the:
questions.explanation: A (Organization test): They weren't organized to capture the value.
